Rebuilt from 40,000 to nearly 95,000 capacity for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, FNB Stadium — known during the tournament as Soccer City — hosted both the opening match and the final, in which Spain beat the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time. Nicknamed "the Calabash" for its resemblance to a traditional African gourd, it is the largest stadium in Africa and was the site of Nelson Mandela's first speech in Johannesburg after his release from prison in 1990.
Of the five stadia used and 32 matches played for the 1970 FIFA World Cup, the largest and most utilised venue was the Azteca Stadium in Mexico City.

The iconic twin-towers Wembley hosted the 1966 FIFA World Cup final on 30 July 1966, where England beat West Germany 4–2 after extra time in front of 96,924 fans. It remains England's only World Cup victory. Geoff Hurst scored a hat-trick — still the only one in a World Cup final — and the match featured one of football's most debated goals, the "Wembley-Tor". The original stadium was demolished in 2003.

Built in just nine months specifically to host the inaugural 1930 FIFA World Cup, the Estadio Centenario hosted ten of the tournament's matches, including both semi-finals and the final, in which Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2. Designed by Juan Scasso and named after the centenary of Uruguay's constitution, it was declared FIFA's first Historical Monument of World Football in 1983 — the only building ever to receive that honour.
